title: ITD 256 Midterm Study Guide
description: Reference notes on database concepts, the relational model and keys, SQL, ERD and Crow's Foot notation, and normalization.

sections.name: Database Concepts, File Systems & Data Models

blocks.text: File & Database Terminology

rows: Raw facts — a phone number, a birth date, a YTD sales figure. Little meaning until organized.
A character or group of characters with a specific meaning. Used to define and store data.
A logically connected set of fields describing one person, place or thing.
A collection of related records — the term used in a **non-DBMS**, file-based system.
A collection of related records. Same definition as File, but called Table inside a **DBMS**.

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: Data → Field → Record → Table. Each level is built out of the one before it, and the right-hand column is the vocabulary you switch to once you start drawing ERDs.
Types of Databases
By degree of data structure

rows: Data in its original, raw state.
Data that results from formatting — structure applied to suit a type of processing.
Partially processed. **XML** (Extensible Markup Language) is the standard example: it represents data elements in a textual format.

blocks.text: By location

rows: Created and maintained with cloud services providing defined performance measures.

blocks.text: By use

rows: Stores historical data and business metrics used **exclusively** for tactical or strategic decision making.
Stores data in a format optimized for decision support.
Online analytical processing — tools to retrieve, process and model data from a data warehouse.
Capturing and processing business data to generate information that supports decisions.

blocks.text: Why File Systems Were Abandoned

items: Manual file systems → computerized file systems → "file system redux": modern productivity tools such as Excel, which quietly bring the old problems back.
Lengthy development times, and difficulty getting quick answers to ad hoc queries.
Challenges with the kinds of information that can be created, and with its accuracy.
**Structural and data dependence** (below), and uncontrolled **data redundancy**.

blocks.text: Structural & Data (In)dependence

rows: Access to a file depends on its own structure, so every program must be modified when the structure changes.
The file structure can change without affecting the application's ability to access the data.
Data access changes when data **storage characteristics** change.
Storage characteristics can change without affecting the program's ability to access data.

blocks.text: The practical significance of data dependence is the difference between two formats. **Logical** = how data is represented to the application or user. **Physical** = how it is actually stored on hardware, which **should be hidden completely and of no concern** to the user.

blocks.label: Compared with file systems:
blocks.text: databases allow for **more data independence**, more robust organization, and better control of data access.
Data Redundancy & Anomalies

**Data redundancy** is unnecessarily storing the same data in different places, creating **islands of information** and raising the probability of different versions of the same data existing at once.

items: Possible results: poor data security, data inconsistency, data-entry errors, data integrity problems, and anomalies.
**Anomalies develop when not all of the required changes in redundant data are made successfully.**

rows: Changed data ends up inconsistent or incomplete — some copies edited, others not.
New data cannot be recorded completely, because an unrelated fact is missing.
Removing one fact partially removes another that only lived in the same row.

blocks.label: Watch for:
blocks.text: these three names are the payoff of normalization. If you can name which anomaly a scenario describes, you can usually also name the dependency causing it.
The Database System Environment

A **database system** is the organization of components that define and regulate the collection, storage, management and use of data. Five components: **hardware, software, people, procedures, data**.
DBMS Functions

rows: Stores definitions of data elements and their relationships.
Includes performance tuning, which ensures efficient performance.
Formats data to conform to logical expectations.
Enforces user security and data privacy.
Algorithms ensuring concurrent access without compromising integrity.
Enables recovery of the database after a failure.
The query language — plus interfaces for programs.
Accept end-user requests across different network environments.

blocks.text: In a **query language**, users specify **what** result they want and the system determines **how** to produce it. **SQL** (Structured Query Language) is the de facto standard, supported by nearly all vendors — with slight variations.
Data Models

**Data modeling** is creating a specific data model for a determined problem domain. A **data model** is a simple representation of complex real-world data structures, useful for supporting that domain.

rows: A person, place, thing or event about which data is collected.
A restriction placed on data; ensures data integrity.

blocks.text: Business rules help identify all four. **Nouns** translate into **entities**; **verbs** translate into **relationships**. **Relationships are always bidirectional** — to fix one you must ask two questions: how many instances of B relate to one instance of A, and how many instances of A relate to one B.

blocks.label: Levels of abstraction:
blocks.text: Chen notation is the **most abstract**, Crow's Foot sits in the middle, and **DDL SQL** is the **least abstract** — it is the implementation itself.
Other Data Models

rows: Based on the **relation** — a table/entity, a matrix of intersecting tuples (rows) and attributes (columns). An **RDBMS** hides its complexities and makes it easier to implement.
Graphical. An **ERD** models database components; an **entity instance** is a row; **connectivity** labels the relationship type.

Data and relationships in a single structure. An **object** is analogous to a record and carries its own operations; a **class** is analogous to an entity/table — a template. The class hierarchy is an upside-down tree where each class has **only one parent**, and **inheritance** passes down methods and attributes.

blocks.label: Logical vs physical model:
blocks.text: the logical model describes what data is stored and how it relates; the physical model describes how that is actually implemented and stored. Same distinction as logical vs physical format under data independence.
What Keys Are For

A key is one or more attributes that **determine** other attributes. Keys ensure each row is uniquely identifiable, and they establish relationships among tables and ensure data integrity. That word *determine* is the same one that drives the whole of normalization in Part 3.

rows: The attribute or combination of attributes that uniquely identifies a row.
A key composed of more than one attribute.
An attribute that is part of a key. (Attributes in no key at all are **nonprime**.)
Any key that can uniquely identify a row.
A **minimal** superkey — remove any attribute and it stops identifying rows.
A real-world identifier already familiar to users and part of the day-to-day business vocabulary. Can be used as the PK.
A made-up / artificial key, e.g. auto_number.
The primary key of one table placed in another to create a common attribute.
A key used strictly for data retrieval purposes.

blocks.label: Use a surrogate key when:
blocks.text: there is no natural key suitable as a primary key; the primary key would be a composite key with multiple data types; or the primary key would be too long to be usable.
Integrity Rules

rows: All primary key entries are **unique**, and **no part of a primary key may be null**. Every row has its own identity.
No invoice can have a duplicate number, nor can the number be null.
A foreign key may have **either a null entry, or one matching primary key value** in the related table.
A customer might not yet have an assigned sales representative — but it is impossible to have an **invalid** one.

blocks.text: Enforcing referential integrity also makes it impossible to delete a row in one table whose primary key has **mandatory** matching foreign key values in another. That is why you delete children before parents.

blocks.label: NULL
blocks.text: is the absence of any data value. It can mean an **unknown** value, a **known but missing** value, or an **inapplicable** condition. It is not zero and not an empty string — which is why finding it needs `IS NULL` rather than `= NULL`.
Data Dictionary, System Catalog & Schema

rows: A description of all tables in the database, created by the user and designer.
The **system** data dictionary — describes all objects in the database.
The complete **logical view**: the full description of the database.

blocks.text: Relationship Types & How They're Implemented

rows: The **norm** for relational databases. Put the foreign key on the **many** side, referencing the PK on the one side.
One entity relates to only one other. The FK goes on either side — usually the one whose participation is optional.
Create a new **connecting entity** in 1:M relationships with both originals.

blocks.text: That connecting entity is called a **composite entity**, a **bridge table**, or an **associative entity** — three names for the same thing. It **includes the primary keys of the tables to be linked, as foreign keys**, and those two columns together usually form its composite primary key.
Why M:N cannot be done with foreign keys alone

To assign one employee to projects 1, 2 and 3, you would have to write `1,2,3` into the single `proj_id` field — violating the atomic attribute rule. The same problem appears from the other direction when assigning many employees to one project. So a third table is required, storing one row per combination:

ASSIGNMENT
emp_id  proj_id      <- both FKs; together the composite PK
   1        1
   1        2
   2        1
   3        3

blocks.label: In ERM,
blocks.text: an M:N relationship **is valid at the conceptual level**. It is for the logical model — the ERD itself — that you need the bridge table.
Which Side Gets the Foreign Key

For many DEPARTMENTs in each DIVISION (1:M), the FK must be on the **many** side — so `division_id` goes in DEPARTMENT. Putting `department_id` in DIVISION would only ever allow one department per division.

Department                 Division
department_id  division_id     division_id
     1              1              1
     2              3              2
     3              2              3

SELECT * FROM division JOIN department USING (division_id);

blocks.label: Summary:
blocks.text: tables are the basic building blocks of a relational database; keys are central to using them; **each table row must have a primary key**; and although tables are independent, they can be linked by common attributes — foreign keys.
Command Categories

blocks.label: In short:
blocks.text: SQL has essentially **two** sets of commands — DDL and DML. It is nonprocedural, with a basic vocabulary of fewer than 100 words.
DDL Reference

rows: Permanently delete an entire database, including all tables.
Create a new table in the user's schema.
Create a new table from the result of a query.
Modify a table definition — add, modify or delete attributes or constraints.
Permanently delete a table **and its data**.
Create or delete an index for a table.
Create or delete a dynamic subset of rows and columns from one or more tables.
Ensure a column has no null values.
Ensure a column has no duplicate values.
Define the table's primary key, or a foreign key.
Define a value used when none is given.

blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE workshop (
  workshop_id   INTEGER,
  workshop_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  seat_limit    INTEGER DEFAULT 12,
  branch_id     INTEGER,
  PRIMARY KEY (workshop_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (branch_id) REFERENCES branch(branch_id)
);

blocks.label: DROP vs DELETE:
blocks.text: `DROP TABLE` is DDL and removes the structure along with the data. `DELETE FROM` is DML and removes rows, leaving the table in place.
SELECT Statement Anatomy

SELECT   columnlist
FROM     tablelist
[WHERE    conditionlist]
[GROUP BY columnlist]
[HAVING   conditionlist]
[ORDER BY columnlist [ASC | DESC]];

rows: Specifies the attributes to be returned.
Specifies the table(s) data is retrieved from.
Groups rows into collections sharing the same values in one or more attributes.
Filters the **groups** formed by GROUP BY.
Sorts the final result rows, ascending (default) or descending.

blocks.label: WHERE vs HAVING:
blocks.text: WHERE filters rows **before** grouping, so an aggregate like `count(*)` cannot appear in it — the groups do not exist yet. HAVING filters groups **after**, so that is where aggregate conditions belong.

**DISTINCT** produces a list of only unique values. The **`*`** wildcard stands in for every column. Dates are stored as a number of days, so **date arithmetic** is possible in a query — though date comparisons are often more software-specific than other SQL.
Cascading ORDER BY

SELECT gadget_title, daily_fee
FROM gadget
ORDER BY daily_fee DESC, gadget_title;

-- daily_fee sorts high to low; gadget_title breaks the ties,
-- ascending, because DESC applies only to the column it follows.
WHERE Clause Operators

rows: Less than / less than or equal to
Greater than / greater than or equal to
Whether a value falls in an **inclusive** range.
Whether a value appears in a list. Shorthand for a chain of ORs.
Whether text matches a pattern. `%` = any run of characters.
Whether a value is absent. The **only** way to test for null.

blocks.text: Logical operators **AND, OR and NOT** combine multiple conditions. Old-style joins written as `WHERE table1.pk = table2.fk` still work but are **generally not recommended**: they make complex queries harder to maintain and are susceptible to undetected errors.
Joins

rows: Only rows from both tables that match on the common value.
The matched rows **plus** unmatched rows from one table or the other. ANSI defines **left**, **right** and **full**.

Rows matching on identically named, type-compatible columns — with the duplicate column eliminated. If there are no common attributes it returns the relational product, which is almost never what you wanted.
A table joined to **itself**. Unary; every other join is binary.

blocks.text:
-- USING: the key has the same name in both tables
SELECT locality_name, region_name
FROM locality
INNER JOIN region USING (region_id);

-- ON: spell out the condition; needed when the names differ
SELECT b.branch_label, l.locality_name
FROM branch b
INNER JOIN locality l ON b.locality_id = l.locality_id;

-- Chaining three tables through a bridge (an M:N relationship)
SELECT gadget_title
FROM gadget
INNER JOIN gadget_group_map USING (gadget_id)
INNER JOIN gadget_group     USING (group_id)
WHERE gadget_group.group_label = 'Plumbing';
Outer joins find what is missing

-- Patrons who have never borrowed anything.
-- An INNER join could never show these rows: there is nothing to match.
SELECT p.patron_id, p.surname
FROM patron p
LEFT JOIN checkout c ON c.patron_id = p.patron_id
WHERE c.checkout_id IS NULL;
Recursive (self) join

-- Both the worker and the boss are rows in the same table,
-- so the aliases are what make two copies of it distinguishable.
SELECT worker.surname AS steward,
       boss.surname   AS reports_to
FROM steward worker
INNER JOIN steward boss ON worker.supervisor_id = boss.steward_id;

blocks.label: Aliases:
blocks.text: an alias identifies the source table a column came from, improves maintainability, and is **required** for a self-join. The most common cause of duplicate column names across joined tables is the existence of a foreign key.
Aggregates & Grouping

rows: The total of a numeric column.

blocks.text: An aggregate query **takes a collection of rows and reduces it to a single row**. Add GROUP BY and you get one row per group instead. Any column in the SELECT list that is not aggregated has to appear in the GROUP BY.

SELECT power_source,
       count(*)               AS how_many,
       round(avg(daily_fee),2) AS avg_fee
FROM gadget
GROUP BY power_source
HAVING count(*) > 5
ORDER BY power_source;
Data Manipulation (DML)

blocks.label: SQL does not ask for confirmation.
blocks.text: An UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause hits **every row in the table**. Always use WHERE with UPDATE to specify which rows, and with DELETE to limit the damage.
**CRUD** = Create, Read, Update, Delete → **(C) INSERT** adds new rows, **(R) SELECT** reads them, **(U) UPDATE** modifies existing rows, **(D) DELETE** gets rid of rows.
Basic ANSI **data types**, supported by all vendors in different ways: NUMBER, NUMERIC, INTEGER, CHAR, VARCHAR, DATE.
Harborview Tool Library

The **SQL Playground** on the home page runs a real SQLite database inside your browser — nothing is installed, nothing is uploaded, and the **Reset** button puts the data back whenever you want. Run whatever you like in it, including INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

The scenario: a community tool-lending library. Members (**patrons**) borrow physical **units** of a catalog **gadget** from a **branch**; the staff are **stewards**. It deliberately has the same *shapes* as the standard textbook examples — a catalog, physical copies, loans, payments, a many-to-many category link, and a self-referencing staff hierarchy — under completely different names, so you have to read the schema rather than recall it.

Every SQL question in the quiz is checked by actually running your query against this database and comparing the rows it returns, so a different-but-correct query still scores. Use **Run** as often as you like while you work it out.

rows: 12 staff; supervisor_id points at another steward
**Bridge** resolving the M:N between gadgets and groups
280 loans; returned_on is NULL while still out
417 charges — loan fees, late fees, dues

blocks.label: Referential integrity is switched on.
blocks.text: Try `DELETE FROM patron WHERE patron_id = 1;` in the playground — it will be refused, because that patron has loans and ledger entries pointing at them. That refusal *is* referential integrity — worth seeing happen at least once.
Getting to the answer

items: **Which tables hold the columns I was asked for?** If they are in two tables, you are joining.
**How do those tables connect?** Follow the foreign keys in the schema panel. Sometimes you have to hop through a third table — a steward has no locality, so you reach it via branch.
**Row filter or group filter?** A condition on a plain column is WHERE; a condition on a count or total is HAVING.
**Did the question say unique?** Then DISTINCT. Joining to the many side duplicates rows.
**Did the question say sort?** Then ORDER BY — and add a second column if the first one has ties.

blocks.label: MySQL vs the browser engine:
blocks.text: the playground runs SQLite, with `MONTH()`, `YEAR()`, `DAY()`, `LEFT()`, `RIGHT()`, `DATEDIFF()`, `CURDATE()` and `NOW()` added so the MySQL forms work. `CONCAT()` works, and so does SQLite's `||`. Everything else here is standard SQL that behaves the same in both.
The Connector Options Legend

Crow's Foot ERDs mark each end of a relationship line with one of six connectors, built from three symbols: a **circle** (zero), a **bar** (one) and a **crow's foot** (many). Read from the outside in: the outer symbol is the **minimum** (participation), the inner symbol is the **maximum** (cardinality).

A   ───<        many
B   ──|<        one or many
C   ──o<        zero or many
D   ───|        one
E   ──||        one and only one
F   ──o|        zero or one

blocks.label: The two-question habit:
blocks.text: a circle always means the relationship is optional at that end. A crow's foot always means many. Everything else follows.
Reading a Business Rule Into a Connector

items: Pick **one end** of the line and stand at the *other* entity, looking toward it.
Ask **must it, or may it?** — "must have" / "must be" means minimum one (bar). "May or may not" means minimum zero (circle).
Ask **one, or many?** — "only one" / "exactly one" means maximum one (bar). "Many" means maximum many (crow's foot).
Combine the two symbols and read off the letter.
Now walk to the other end and do it again. **Relationships are bidirectional**, and one sentence rarely settles both ends.

blocks.text: Worked example
"A DEPOT must store at least one CRATE, and can store many. Every CRATE must be stored at exactly one DEPOT."

items: **CRATE end** (looking from DEPOT): must store at least one → minimum one, bar. Can store many → maximum many, crow's foot. Bar + crow's foot = **B**.
**DEPOT end** (looking from CRATE): must be stored at → minimum one, bar. Exactly one → maximum one, bar. Two bars = **E**.
Cardinality is therefore **1:M**, and `depot_id` goes in CRATE — the many side.

blocks.text: A second example, with an optional end
"Some technicians, known as 'floaters', are not assigned to any WORKSHOP. Any technician who is assigned belongs to just one."

items: **WORKSHOP end**: a floater has none → minimum zero, circle. An assigned technician has one → maximum one, bar. Circle + bar = **F**.
The `workshop_id` column in TECHNICIAN must therefore **allow nulls** — which referential integrity permits.

blocks.text: Reading Entity Boxes
An entity box has a header holding the entity name, then rows. The narrow left-hand cells hold the key markers; the wide right-hand cells hold the attribute names:

rows: The label **PK** or **FK** for the row beside it

blocks.label: Even when the business rules describe no attributes at all,
blocks.text: the ERD still needs the primary and foreign key fields — those are what carry the relationships.
Turning Relationships Into Keys

rows: The PK of the *one* side, repeated as an FK on the *many* side. Nothing changes on the one side.
The PK of one side as an FK in the other — normally in the table whose participation is optional.
A **bridge entity**. It holds both PKs as FKs, and those two columns together are its composite PK. One M:N line becomes **two 1:M lines**.
An FK column in the table that references that same table's own PK. The top of the hierarchy has a null there.

blocks.label: Why the FK cannot go on the "one" side:
blocks.text: a single column holds a single value. To point at many children you would have to stuff several key values into one field, which is exactly the atomicity violation that forces a bridge table in the M:N case.

Two entities can also be joined by **more than one** relationship line. STEWARD and BRANCH carry both "works at" (1:M) and "manages" (1:1) — two separate relationships between the same pair of entities, each with its own connectors.
Normal Forms
**Normalization** is evaluating and correcting table structures to **minimize redundancies**, which reduces data anomalies. It assigns attributes to tables based on **determination**.

rows: Table format, **no repeating groups**, and the primary key is identified. All attributes depend on the PK.
**Every determinant is a candidate key.** A special case of 3NF.
In 3NF and no independent multivalued dependencies.

blocks.label: Shortcut:
blocks.text: if a 1NF table's primary key is a **single** attribute, it is automatically in 2NF — a partial dependency needs *part* of a composite key, and a one-column key has no parts. You still have to check for transitive dependencies.
Key Vocabulary

rows: B is functionally dependent on A if **each value of A determines one and only one value of B**. Written A → B.
The attribute on the **left** of the arrow — it does the determining.
The attribute on the **right** of the arrow.
A determines B if **all rows that agree in value for A also agree in value for B**. This is the version you can test against sample data.
B depends on composite key A but **not on any subset** of A.
A functional dependence whose determinant is **only part of the PK**. Requires a composite key.
An attribute dependent on **another non-key attribute**. Occurs only among nonprime attributes — which is what makes it harder to spot.
Several columns holding the same kind of fact (phone1, phone2, phone3), or several values crammed into one cell. Breaks 1NF.

blocks.text: The Procedure

items: Write down the **primary key**. If it is composite, note both parts separately — you will need them.
Find the attributes that depend on the **whole** key. Those stay where they are.
Find every attribute that depends on **part** of the key. Each such determinant becomes a **new table**, keyed on that determinant, taking everything it determines with it. That is 2NF.

Inside each remaining table, look for an attribute determined by **another non-key attribute**. Split that determinant out into its own table too, and **leave the determinant behind as a foreign key**. That is 3NF.
Check: in every table, does each non-key attribute depend on **the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key**?

blocks.label: "The whole key"
blocks.text: catches partial dependencies. **"Nothing but the key"** catches transitive ones. That one sentence is most of what normalization asks of you.
Worked Example
**CATERING_ORDER** in 1NF, primary key **booking_ref + dish_code**:

CATERING_ORDER(booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name,
               client_city, dish_code, dish_name, dish_style,
               dish_price, portions)
Step 1 — the dependency set

(booking_ref, dish_code) -> portions            (full — needs both halves)

booking_ref -> booking_date, client_no,
               client_name, client_city         (partial)
dish_code   -> dish_name, dish_style,
               dish_price                       (partial)

client_no   -> client_name, client_city         (transitive)

How many portions were ordered needs both halves of the key. Everything about the booking follows from `booking_ref` alone; everything about the dish follows from `dish_code` alone. And the client's name and city follow from `client_no`, which is itself just an ordinary attribute of the booking.
Step 2 — 2NF (partial dependencies removed)

BOOKING(booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city)
DISH(dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price)
BOOKING_LINE(booking_ref, dish_code, portions)

-- PK of BOOKING_LINE is (booking_ref, dish_code);
-- both columns are also FKs, to BOOKING and DISH.
Step 3 — 3NF (transitive dependency removed)

CLIENT(client_no, client_name, client_city)
BOOKING(booking_ref, booking_date, client_no)      -- client_no is now an FK
DISH(dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price)
BOOKING_LINE(booking_ref, dish_code, portions)

Only the first two tables changed between 2NF and 3NF: `client_no → client_name, client_city` came out of BOOKING into its own CLIENT table, with `client_no` left behind as the foreign key linking them.
Second Worked Example
**SEMINAR_ROSTER** in 1NF, primary key **seminar_code + attendee_id**, where each seminar meets in exactly one room:

SEMINAR_ROSTER(seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity,
               attendee_id, attendee_name, attendee_email, grade)

Dependency set:
(seminar_code, attendee_id) -> grade                          (full)
seminar_code -> seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity       (partial)
attendee_id  -> attendee_name, attendee_email                 (partial)
room_code    -> room_capacity                                 (transitive)

3NF:
ROOM(room_code, room_capacity)
SEMINAR(seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code)               -- room_code FK
ATTENDEE(attendee_id, attendee_name, attendee_email)
ENROLLMENT(seminar_code, attendee_id, grade)                  -- both FKs, composite PK

blocks.label: Worth noticing:
blocks.text: ENROLLMENT is exactly the **bridge entity** you would have drawn on an ERD for the M:N between seminars and attendees. Normalization and ER modeling arrive at the same table from opposite directions.
Spotting the Two Dependencies

rows: Part of the composite primary key
Nothing in particular — any key at all
Cover half the key: is the attribute still determined?
Look for a chain among ordinary attributes: PK → X → Y
The dish's price repeats on every order line; a dish nobody has ordered cannot be recorded
The client's details repeat on every booking; deleting their last booking erases the client

blocks.text: Both are fixed the same way: **move the determinant and everything it determines into a new table, and leave the determinant behind as a foreign key.**
Denormalization
Denormalization deliberately produces a **lower** normal form, trading increased data redundancy for better performance.

blocks.label: The trade-off:
blocks.text: more tables require more I/O operations and processing logic to join them. Normalization is important — but only **part** of the design process, and designers are often forced into compromises.
